title: Funerals
hook: from Orthodox memory eternal to Protestant celebrations of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, ars moriendi, the art of dying. Your line was die well, live well. Did you loosen your grip on one grudge before you slept? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

Two funerals on the same Saturday. In the first, an Orthodox church, the coffin is open, candles are lit in every hand, and the air is thick with incense. At the end the choir sings one short line, slow and low, again and again, and the whole room joins in. In the second, a Protestant church across town, there's a slideshow on a screen: a man at a barbecue, a man holding a grandchild, a man in a terrible sweater. People laugh. Someone reads a poem. A friend tells a story about a fishing trip that went wrong. Two rooms, two moods, the same faith underneath. Today's word is what happens in both.

A Christian funeral is doing two jobs at once: grieving a person, and saying out loud what the church hopes. Churches balance those jobs differently. First, the Orthodox. Their funeral and memorial services end with a short hymn, memory eternal. It sounds like a wish that people won't forget. It's more than that. It asks God to remember the one who has died. In Genesis, "God remembered Noah," and the next thing God does is make a wind pass over the earth, and the waters go down. Second, the Catholic funeral Mass. The body is brought into church, often sprinkled with holy water and covered with a white cloth that recalls baptism, and the Mass is offered for the person who has died. Third, Protestant churches. A service of witness to the resurrection, or what some families call a celebration of life: hymns, scripture, and stories that bring the person back into the room for an hour. Fourth, what they share. At graveside, an old English prayer book has the minister commit the body "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the Resurrection to eternal life." The same prayer book opens its burial service with words Jesus spoke to Martha, on his way to her brother Lazarus's grave: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Different rooms. Candles or slideshows. Tears or laughter, usually both. Underneath, the same claim: this person is not lost to God.
screen: `EARTH TO EARTH, IN SURE AND CERTAIN HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a funeral. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one you attended, or one you missed and wish you hadn't. Where were you standing? What was sung or said? Who did you hug? Then bring the person back to mind, one clear detail: a laugh, a habit, a phrase they used. Hold it. If you pray, you can say their name to God and ask God to remember them. If you don't, simply keep their memory company for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Funerals. The church's way of grieving a person and naming its hope in the same hour, from the Orthodox memory eternal to a Protestant celebration of life.

Your line: memory eternal. This week went from date-setters and painted apocalypses, through the saints marching in, hope over fear, numbering our days and the art of dying, to the funeral. Today, say one name out loud that you don't want lost. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Orthodox funerals and memorial services end with the hymn Memory Eternal; Catholics celebrate a funeral Mass; Protestant churches hold a service of worship with hymns, scripture and remembrance, sometimes called a celebration of life.

notes: Day 1323 is a week end: the carry looks back over days 1317–1323.
Orthodox details (open coffin, candles held by mourners, incense, Memory Eternal sung at the end) given as one scene, not as universal practice. Confirm.
Catholic details: holy water and the white pall recalling baptism; 'often' used. Confirm.
'Celebration of life' attributed to 'some families'; 'service of witness to the resurrection' is a phrase from some Protestant books of worship. Confirm fair.
The theological point that God's 'remembering' in scripture means acting (e.g., Genesis 8:1, God remembered Noah) is paraphrased; confirm.
BCP 1662 committal wording quoted; confirm exact text.
Original: Greek Αἰωνία ἡ μνήμη; in Slavonic usage the hymn is Vechnaya pamyat. Confirm spelling and transliteration.

Editor pass: replaced the sweeping 'in the Bible, when God remembers someone, God acts' with Genesis 8:1 itself (God remembered Noah, then made a wind pass over the earth); corrected John 11:25 as spoken to Martha on the way to Lazarus's grave, not at it, and tied it to the BCP 1662 burial service, which opens with those words; dropped 'now' from 'celebration of life'; replaced 'across these churches you'll hear'.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): "the choir sings three words" was true only of the Greek (Αἰωνία ἡ μνήμη); in English and Slavonic it is two, so it now says "one short line". The review's "set a grudge down" echoed day 1317's fear set down on a table; now matches 1322's "loosen your hold".
